notes.text: Photoacoustic infrared fits the first row. Hydrides are dominated by colorimetric tape systems and are not ThermGAS's market.
ThermGAS's semiconductor page says its systems can be configured for SF6, NF3, C4F6 and CF4. It names no model.

ThermGAS's Master Gas List (Sep 2026) includes NF3, C4F6 (hexafluoro-1,3-butadiene), C4F8, SF6 and hexafluoropropylene. It shows no detection levels, and it does not list CF4 or fluorinated heat-transfer fluids such as HT-200, FC-3283 or HFE-7500.

NF3 exposure limits are 10 ppm as an 8-hour average (OSHA PEL, NIOSH REL, and an ACGIH TLV from a 1993-94 listing); NIOSH's revised IDLH is 1,000 ppm. Honeywell's NF3 cartridge allows a minimum first alarm of 4 ppm.

entry_points.summary: The best fit is NF3 and C4F6 around CVD and etch tools, plus the facility chiller plant, which is ThermGAS's home ground.

transfers.text: Haloguard IR's multi-point scanning (up to 24 points) suits clusters of tools or gas cabinets.
TracePoint 1000 is a single-point monitor that can sit close to a tool; its page lists a 0-1000 ppm range, a 4-20 mA output and 150 ft of standard sample tubing.
A photoacoustic monitor has no electrolyte cartridge or pyrolyzer to replace (Honeywell's NF3 path has both), which matters where every sensor swap needs cleanroom access.

players.name: Honeywell
players.product_line: Midas NF3 path (pyrolyzer + cartridge); Vertex Edge

they_win.text: Midas NF3 path: pyrolyzer module plus electrochemical cartridge, 0-40 ppm, response under 110 s, 24-month cartridge life (data sheet dated November 2019).
Vertex Edge: up to nine Chemcassette analyzers with eight points each, for virtually every gas used in fabs, down to ppb.

thermgas_can_win.text: Honeywell's NF3 path needs a pyrolyzer, a cartridge replaced about every 24 months and calibration about every 6 months. A photoacoustic monitor has no cartridge to replace, but ThermGAS publishes no NF3 maintenance data.
Honeywell's cartridge reads chlorine, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen fluoride and sulphur dioxide as NF3. A selective optical method might avoid that, but ThermGAS has not published a test.

watch_out.text: Not a solvent problem: Honeywell's sheet shows isopropanol and methanol at 500 ppm reading 0. A solvent false-alarm pitch would be answered with Honeywell's own data.
Covers almost every fab gas, so a fab can standardise on one supplier.

head_to_head.takeaway: On published data, Honeywell's NF3 path has documented figures and ThermGAS has none that are NF3-specific. The solvent argument is not supported: Honeywell's sheet shows no response to isopropanol or methanol. The sheet is dated November 2019, so check the current revision. A defensible ThermGAS argument is no cartridge or pyrolyzer to maintain, and possibly less acid-gas interference, but both need ThermGAS tests.

checks: EPA's sector page was read: 46 facilities reported in 2023 (56 in 2011, 53 in 2016). It covers semiconductors, LEDs, MEMS, LCDs and solar, so 46 is not a fab count.
The brief's 53-fab size mix for 2023 and its "65 since 2011" could not be matched to EPA's table (which shows 53 facilities in 2016). Neither is used as a headline figure.
ThermGAS's Master Gas List PDF (Sep 2026) was read and its layout checked: NF3, C4F6, C4F8 and SF6 are listed; CF4, HT-200, FC-3283 and HFE-7500 are not. No detection levels are shown.
The NF3 and C4F6 application note cited by the team brief was not found on thermgas.com or through web search.

Honeywell's NF3 cartridge sheet (SS01115K_v5, November 2019) and RKI's GD-70D data sheet were read. A search result suggested a regional Honeywell page marks the Midas pyrolyzer out of production; the page text could not confirm it, so it is not stated.

The brief's claim that pyrolyzer detectors false-alarm on cleaning solvents is not supported by Honeywell's sheet (isopropanol and methanol read 0). Its cross-sensitivities are chlorine, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen fluoride, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide.
MSA's Chemgard is documented only by a 2014 press release; NF3 support and current status are unverified (a trade-press page was blocked).
NF3 exposure limits come from NIOSH's IDLH page; the ACGIH value is from a 1993-94 listing.
The $52.3B figure covers computer, electronics and electrical plants, not only fabs.

note.text: In July 2025 the administration exempted 41 facilities from EPA's 2024 sterilizer rule, and in March 2026 EPA proposed letting sterilizers choose continuous or parametric monitoring. Workplace exposure limits still apply, which is why this page does not lead with ethylene oxide.
